name: Barbarika
role: Folk hero worshipped as Khatu Shyam
summary: Barbarika is a hero of folk and Puranic tradition, described as a grandson of Bhima. Devotees worship him as Khatu Shyam, the 'support of those who have lost'.
about: Barbarika does not appear in the main text of the Mahabharata, but regional tradition and some Puranic accounts describe him as the son of Ghatotkacha and a grandson of Bhima. He is known for a bow with three arrows that never fail. In the widely told folk version, Krishna tests him before the Kurukshetra War and asks for his head as a gift, which Barbarika gives so long as he may watch the battle. Devotees say Krishna then blessed him to be worshipped as Shyam in the Kali Yuga. He is revered at Khatu in Rajasthan, as Baliyadev in Gujarat and in Nepal, where he is linked with Yalambar and Akash Bhairav. Tellings differ, and the Skanda Purana has its own version.
kidSummary: Barbarika is a brave hero from folk stories, said to be Bhima's grandson. He had a bow with three special arrows. The story tells that he gave up something very precious to Krishna, and so today many people visit his temple at Khatu in Rajasthan and call him Shyam Baba.

story.title: A hero with three arrows
story.text: The story tells of Barbarika, a young warrior and Bhima's grandson, who carries a bow and three special arrows that do not miss.

story.title: A promise to help the weaker side
story.text: In a folk telling, he promises to join whichever side is losing in the coming war. Krishna, dressed as a Brahmin, tests him and asks him a question.

story.title: A hidden leaf
story.text: In popular retellings, Barbarika's arrow marks every leaf on a tree, including one that Krishna hides under his foot, and Krishna sees how powerful the arrows are.

story.title: A hard gift
story.text: Krishna explains that the promise could cause endless fighting. In the popular version, he asks Barbarika for his head as a gift, and Barbarika gives it gladly.

story.title: A seat to watch
story.text: Barbarika's head watches the war from a hill. Krishna blesses him, and people worship him as Shyam.

teaches: Thinking about what a promise really leads to
Standing by those who need support

facts.text: In the Skanda Purana (Kaumarika Khanda, chapter 60, in Tagare's translation) he gets his name from his hair, which looked like that of the Barbara people. He grows into a young man the moment he is born, bows to his parents and asks them to name him.

In the Skanda Purana, a stranger washing in a holy pond angers Barbarika, who guards it. Neither knows the other. They wrestle, and he lifts the tiring man toward the sea until Rudra calls from the sky that it is his grandfather Bhima.

A Nepali telling says Barbarika came to watch the war, vowing to join whichever side was losing. Krishna reasoned that this vow, backed by three arrows, would leave only Barbarika alive, so he cut off his head by a clever stroke.

In the Skanda Purana, Bhishma and Kripa promise to end the war in a month, Drona in a fortnight, Ashvatthama in ten days and Karna in six, and Arjuna says one day. Barbarika then says he can do it in a single muhurta.

In the Skanda Purana, to prove it, he fires an arrow trailing ash that lands on the one weak spot of every warrior in both armies, such as Bhishma's hair, Karna's neck and Duryodhana's thigh. It misses only the Pandavas, Kripa and Ashvatthama.

In the Skanda Purana, Krishna beheads him with the discus mid-speech. Chandika then explains: the yaksha Suryavarcas boasted he alone could lift Earth's burden, so Brahma cursed him to fall by Krishna's hand, and Vishnu promised his head would be worshipped.

In the Skanda Purana, after his death Chandika sprinkles nectar on his head, making it unageing. It asks to watch the battle and is told to climb a mountain peak. Krishna promises he will be adored for as long as the earth, moon and sun last.
Krishna remarks in the Skanda Purana that Barbarika is already known for killing a demon named Palashi and his nine crore rakshasa followers in Patala in a single moment.

In the Skanda Purana he is so ashamed on learning that he fought his own grandfather that he walks into the sea to end his life. The sea trembles, and the goddesses steady him and tell him that a deed done in ignorance is no sin.

In the Skanda Purana, after the war Bhima claims the credit while Arjuna says he saw only a Man leading the fight. Asked, Barbarika's head describes one mighty figure bearing the signs of both Shiva and Vishnu, and flowers rain from the sky.

Devotees believe the Khatu Shyam Temple in Sikar district, Rajasthan, holds his head. By local tradition the ruler Roop Singh Chauhan built the first temple in about 1027 CE after a dream led him to a buried idol, found near a pond called Shyam Kund.

The Falgun Mela, around February to March, draws lakhs of devotees, and the temple sees millions each year. In the Nishaan Yatra, pilgrims walk about 17 km from Reengus carrying triangular saffron, orange or red flags to offer.
The Surajgarh flag, which shows a blue horse, is carried on foot for about 152 km to Khatu and raised on the temple during the fair. By tradition this has been done for over 300 years.
Nepal has a parallel tradition. The first Kirata king Yalambar, said to have lived around 800 BCE, is identified with Barbarika, and his head is worshipped as Akash Bhairav in Kathmandu.
Alf Hiltebeitel's study of the epics, cited on Wikipedia's Barbarika page, records that the goddess Durga gave him the three infallible arrows.
Devotees call him Hare Ka Sahara, 'the support of those who are losing', and Teenbaan Dhaari, 'the bearer of three arrows'. Both titles are listed for him on his Wikipedia page.
In the Skanda Purana's council scene, the ash from his arrow falls even on the sole of Krishna's own foot, which the text lists with the weak spots of Bhishma, Karna and Duryodhana.

In the Skanda Purana, Barbarika guards the sage Vijaya's fire rite through the night. In the first watch he catches a blood-clothed demoness named Mahajihva by the throat, then lets her go when she begs and vows to turn to penance.

In the Skanda Purana's night-watch episode, a demon named Repalendra with a hundred heads and a hundred bellies attacks the rite. Barbarika fights him with arrows, swords and fists, and the text says a village called Repalendra stands near the spot even today.

In the same chapter, a huge she-mule named Duhadruha, called queen of the shakinis, charges at the rite. Barbarika rides her, throws her down, and the text says a village named after her exists even today.

In the Skanda Purana, the serpents led by Vasuki thank him for destroying Palashi and offer any boon. Barbarika asks for nothing for himself and requests only that Vijaya's rite be free of every obstacle.

In the Skanda Purana, young Barbarika reaches Dvaraka with his father. Soldiers who keep 900,000 chariots ready in every village sound the alarm at two flying rakshasas, until Ghatotkacha calls out who they are and Krishna embraces them.
The Nepali tradition that identifies Barbarika with the Kirata king Yalambar says his dynasty ruled the Kathmandu valley for about 31 generations, roughly 1,225 years, before the Licchavis followed.

In the Skanda Purana, Chandika's nectar makes his head as deathless as the head of Rahu. The text adds that funeral rites were performed for his body alone and not for the head, which then climbs the peak to watch the war.

The Skanda Purana says that when Brahma cursed the yaksha Suryavarcas, he asked Vishnu for one boon, an intellect that finishes every task from birth. Vishnu agreed and promised that people would worship his head.

quiz.q: How many special arrows is Barbarika known for?
quiz.why: His emblem is a bow with three arrows.

quiz.q: Where is the famous Khatu Shyam Temple?
quiz.why: It is in Khatu, Sikar district, Rajasthan.

quiz.q: Whose grandson is Barbarika said to be?
quiz.why: He is Ghatotkacha's son and Bhima's grandson.

quiz.q: In the folk story, who tests Barbarika disguised as a Brahmin?
quiz.why: In the folk story Krishna, in disguise, tests him with a hidden leaf and then asks for his head.

quiz.q: What does the title Hare Ka Sahara mean?
options: Friend of the lost or defeated
quiz.why: It means a support to those who have lost.
